title: Sesshin
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating mindfulness and presence in everyday life to counteract feelings of frustration, anxiety, or attachment to specific outcomes. By stopping and being present with whatever arises, we can develop greater freedom, compassion, and understanding of ourselves and the world around us. This approach, often referred to as "non-way" or "non-method," allows for a kind of liberation from our tendency to control and optimize life, revealing its complexity and unpredictability in all its beauty and wonder.

sentences.text: So in the political resistance, what's been crowded off the headlines is that apparently our Senate on Monday night, late into the evening, had a vote on an 80 billion dollar increase in the military budget, to nearly 700 billion dollars.
Apparently it's gotten that high before, at the peak of the Afghan and Iraqi wars.
So this is not the first time it's been this obscene, but it does seem on the obscene side.
The 700 billion dollar military budget is more than the next ten largest militaries combined, and represents 30% of global military spending, as one country.
And if you feel a little partisan, you might think, well, those sneaky Republicans, they got it through.
But actually the vote was 89 or 90, something like that, to four.
And both of our Senators voted for this huge military increase, as did most Democratic Senators.
So anyway, I'm going to say this out loud, so maybe I'll actually do it: I'm intending to call Patty Murray's office and Maria Cantwell's office and just say, why?
Can you explain to me?
I don't understand.
When Bernie Sanders proposed universal free education, he was laughed off the block by the Democratic Party, and that would have cost about 48 billion dollars.
So this is almost twice, a little less than twice that.
So it's a tough world we're in, very activating, very confusing.
We don't know what to do, and would our doing something really make a difference anyway?
It seems like it also helps us to stop, with a lot of support, and to have a practice that helps us really feel to the bottom.
This is the practice of sesshin.
I think it's not in lieu of whatever action we feel moved to take, but in support of action.
It helps us make action that's a little more grounded, a little more based on a feeling for life, a little less reactive and more responsive, I guess.
The word sesshin doesn't exactly mean meditation retreat.
There is a word, Zazenkai, that we're using for [unclear: "Andean"] as half-day sits, and there was one on Sunday.
Anybody go?
Nobody here.
Zazenkai means Zazen day.
So they could have called this Zazen week.
I don't know what that would have been, Zazen something else.
But instead it's called sesshin, which is two characters together.
The first is pronounced Setsu, and the second one is Shin.
When you glue them together, it changes the pronunciation, like most compound words: sesshin.
Setsu means to touch something, to feel something, to be in contact with something.
Shin is a word we hear a lot in our sutras.
Makyahanya Haramita Shingyo, same Shin.
This is the character for heart or mind.
So it's a practice of touching the heart-mind, being in contact with the heart-mind.
It's a practice that can last from one to seven, or sometimes eight or ten days.
We're living together in some way, practicing Zazen and eating and walking and sleeping.
So it's more than just a whole big pile of Zazen, although there's a fair bit of that.
Not as much as you might think.
I was going to count up how many periods or hours.
You're awake maybe 16, 18 hours a day, and it's way less than that.
Maybe it's eight hours, maybe seven hours of total Zazen, something like that.
But it's Zazen alternating with walking meditation, kinhin, with doing services like we just did, with meals that are also taken in a mindful way.
And it's Zazen in the context of silent, continuous practice.
And there's something about being in silence with a shared intention with others that's a big, big part of it somehow.
I have no way of discerning, I can't pull the threads apart, which aspects of sesshin are effective and which are cultural leftovers.
We receive this package, which we've of course modified a little bit to make it work.
But we have no way of knowing: is the benefit from the Zazen, and the rest of it just enables you to stand that much Zazen?
Or is the benefit from the silence?
Is the benefit from the ceremonies?
Is the benefit from all of it together?
Is the benefit from the so-called breaks in the schedule, which usually happen after the meal, where there's an hour-ish, or more or less, of unstructured time?
The thing about it is you have absolutely nothing to do.
How often are we in a quiet place with absolutely nothing to do?
Maybe that's the most important thing of the whole time.
When you're there, you may think, well, why is this important?
I'm just collapsed in a heap, or I'm just going on a walk, whatever.
But maybe that is important too.
A couple of things I thought about sesshin, and then I want to hear what you think about sesshin if you've had the opportunity to practice this way.
One is that we're really good at going, and one going leads to the next going leads to the next going.
I think about it like a chain, or interlocking loops or something.
And by the end of the day you're so exhausted from all this going.
We have a lot of practice and training in going.
We know how to go: go, go, go.
We're skillful at it, and there's a lot of going that needs to happen.
A lot of doing is needed.
We need to somehow meet this world and take care of our life.
But sesshin is an intensive practice in stopping.
For one thing, there's nothing whatsoever you have to figure out or decide.
This does not stop your brain from trying to figure things out and make lots of decisions, but there's nothing you actually do have to figure out or decide at sesshin.
It's all planned out.
Your itinerary is planned.
The meals are planned.
You don't decide what to eat, when to eat, how much.
I guess you could decide a little bit how much to eat, but that's a little bit limited by the format too.
You don't decide what show to watch or what book to read or whether you should call your friend, because if you do the form completely, you're not doing any of those things.
The silence practice includes letting go of reading and talking and gadgets and all those kinds of verbal interactions with others and with yourself.
This is a little bit uncomfortable sometimes because we don't know how to stop.
We literally don't know how to stop.
And so we practice that.
We practice stopping.
The other thing I love about sesshin is it's a powerful sort of yoga on our preferences.
Because we basically think our preferences are perfectly reasonable, and well justified, because we have good taste or kitsch taste or whatever kind of taste we have.
But if we pay attention, I think we have to realize that our preferences in many cases run us a bit more than we like to admit.
Sometimes preferences become so amplified that they become serious psychological problems that really limit people's lives too.
They make us housebound, or afraid of all kinds of things.
I was working with someone the other day with a spider phobia.
I had no idea that spider phobias could be that powerful.
This person had a PhD in psychology and was very talented, blah, blah, blah.
And I found her, this was not at the sesshin, this is another time, basically in tears because there was a great big spider in the bathroom sink.
Wow, that's powerful.
So that's a little difference in a preference, I suppose, but it's all connected because it's the mind, right?
It's the mind making decisions about what's okay, what's not okay, what we want, what we don't want.
What's great about sesshin is that when it's a little quieter, we can see the preference as a preference.
And there's less, I don't know how to say it, less room for the justifications.
You can see the justifications are just that much more stuff, that much more thought.
Or maybe in regular life we're so busy we don't even notice the justifications.
They're operating under the surface and we just run our preferences.
So I'm pretty equanimous about food.
I'm vegetarian, so it makes me a little uncomfortable to eat meat, but otherwise I'm pretty equanimous about food.
This is just a small example, but small examples are where we learn.
But I really have a stronger aversion to peanut butter.
Especially peanut butter baked into stuff.
And sooner or later in sesshin, to cheer us up, they serve us tea and a little cookie in the afternoon.
You're flagging, and then somebody shows up and gives you tea and a cookie.
It's very nice.
But sooner or later in every sesshin they serve peanut butter cookies.
And I can never quite detect the peanut butter cookies before I end up with them.
They're unavoidable, these peanut butter cookies.
So this time, as I try to do every time, and maybe I made a little progress this time, I really tried to just tune in.
Sometimes I just hold my nose and I think, more tea, more tea.
But this time I really tried to pay attention and feel the feeling of eating this peanut butter cookie.
The aversion to the flavor was definitely there, just this inner tension of some kind.
But the chewiness of the cookie was no different from any other cookie, and that's very pleasant.
And the mealiness of the flour and the nuts or whatever was in there.
And just the satisfyingness of chewing.
Chewing is so satisfying.
It feels like we're in contact with something that's nourishing us.

What's so great about sesshin is that all kinds of preferences arise, and in that context it's more possible to notice a preference as a preference, and to study the inner dynamics of a preference: the thoughts and emotions and feelings in the body that arise.
Because the real goal here is not just to have a nice little tool so we're calmer and a little happier.
Well, there's nothing wrong with that.
If that's your goal, go forth.
That's good.
But the real goal of this practice is actually freedom.
And freedom for what?
Freedom to help.
Freedom to live a life of service, connection and love.
Preferences shut down our freedom and make it harder for us to be connected, loving beings.
So preferences come up like crazy sometimes for people.
I really don't like the way she's walking.
Why is she walking that way?
That's so arrogant.
And connected to preferences are projections, of course.
This is great, because we can see our projections so clearly.
In our social talking, we're constantly readjusting our projections so that we think they're accurate.
Without the talking, the projection has lots of room to develop and build until eventually it's demolished by reality.
And so you can see the way you're projecting all kinds of stories on other people.
People fall madly in love with each other and madly in hate with each other.
And then your love object says one word at the end of this machine, one word, and the whole thing just crashes down.
He's not what I thought he was at all.
So this is also a very powerful quality of mind.
It seems to be a quality of mind that we need.
We need some way to make sense of reality, and we're always making sense of reality based on very small bits of information.
Our view of reality is never quite right, but we don't see it because we're so in the middle of it and it's coming at us so fast, and we're constantly adjusting and navigating.
So sitting on your little cushion staring at your neighbor for multiple days, you can see the mind making this stuff up.
Sometimes you see the mind making it up.
Sometimes you believe it.
And then eventually it's destroyed.

So these are experiential trainings in how the mind works, to help us with freedom, to help us with the subtle and infinitely complex and rich actual nature of this human life that we'll never quite know.
It's always richer and more subtle and more complicated than we can quite realize.
It's a very similar thing with planning and choice making.
Our American ideal is, if I could just get to do whatever the hell I wanted, I'd be happy, right?
And it's so distressing to people when the life circumstances are such that they get that and they're not happy.
So can we be free in the middle of the opposite of that?
Free in the middle of not having any choices?
It turns out that you can.
You can really feel that way.
And this is really revealing, because if we can be free in the middle of a situation where we have no choices, what is it that we think can actually bind us?
What could we think would take away our freedom?
I think maybe a couple of weeks ago or sometime we were talking about compassion.
I mean, that was another group.
I don't know.

When I say that, I always think about the amazing stories, and there are many of these stories, of Tibetan practitioners who were locked up and in some cases tortured by the Chinese, the Chinese soldiers who had been ordered to do this stuff.
In many cases these practitioners somehow retained this sense of freedom and didn't demonize their captors.

And of course there are famous examples of this through all kinds of horrible imprisonments and holocausts, and Nelson Mandela for his 18 or 19 years or whatever it was on Robben Island, never giving up on his captors, always being kind to them.
So there's a way that we can learn about freedom that's not contingent on getting what we want.
And sesshin, thankfully, is more gentle than being locked up and tortured.
But it seems like a lesson humans really need to learn, and I don't know of any other way to learn it: that our ideas about freedom are a little upside down.
There are a lot of implications to how we live, and how our economy runs, and our political system, and lots of problems from that.
Another thing, and all this stuff happens week to week here as well, but it's more concentrated, it's more clear at sesshin.
We get to do this for a day or three days or a week.
This next one is pretty clear here, so this one's more portable, I guess.
It's the great learning that comes from when they assign you to a job, like ringing the bells.
Maybe it feels more loaded at sesshin because it's sesshin.
You're sitting there in front of your bell and you get some amount of training, probably not enough, some small amount of training.
And you're expected to hit it at the right time, in the right way, with the right spirit, with the right understanding.
And you can watch your perfectionism and fear and embarrassment and shame, deep stuff.
Of course it's always a little bit funny for the organizers, who are like, I just wanted you to ring the bell.
I'm not intending to activate your deep shame.
You just need a bell.
People need to know it's time to...
We need some shame.
Yeah, we need some shame.
But that's just how it works, we're not in control of all this.
Somehow the service positions, these different jobs that we do at sesshin, can be a rich, rich training in all that.
Or maybe your conditioning is otherwise and you need to learn more about overconfidence or arrogance, and you say, why not I do this?
Then they tell you, no, no, please don't do it that way.
And you get in a big fight with them or something.
Right, it's just a bell.
But one of the great things I've always said about religion, which is the same as sports, I guess...
I was big on sports metaphors this last week at sesshin, because I misheard the ino the first night, so then I studied this all week.
He was, the ino was Ewan, [unclear: "Ewan McGee"].
And he was in his calm sesshin mode, so he wasn't speaking that clearly, actually.
And he said, well, and another sport we have is the schedule.
But actually what he said was support.
But I heard sport.
So I thought, oh, that's right.
This is a sport.
We have, we're all on the team and we're in the field and we've got a job to do together.
We want to perform well, and we have coaches.
Yeah, it's competition.
"She's doing it better than me.
I know I shouldn't feel that way.
She's a worthy athlete.
I should just support her."
So anyway, I was on sports all week.
So like sports, we take these things so seriously, and it's all made up.
It's all made-up human stuff.
The rules are agreed upon, I suppose, but also somewhat arbitrary and subject to change.
So we get upset about things that don't matter, which helps us to understand what being upset is and what matters.
I think that's really important too.
And sesshin is such a great way to see that.
You can see it week to week in our practice just as well, I think.
Another thing I love about sesshin is that we project on other people, but we also project on ourselves.
We have all kinds of theories about how we work, and usually they're pretty simple theories, with sort of linear relationships between variables.
One I thought of is the relationship between sleep and energy.
We think X hours of sleep equals Y joules of energy or something like that, right?
A lot of times people don't, at first at least, sleep that great at sesshin.
People are nodding.
People are nodding.
And then you make this huge suffering in the middle of the night because you are so convinced that tomorrow is going to be awful.
The worst day of your life.
It's going to be embarrassing, you're probably going to fail at sesshin and have to leave.
Because it's two in the morning and you're not sleeping and your mind is predicting all this, based on your simple theory about energy and sleep.
And then, to your weird amazement, the next day goes kind of fine.
Then you actually sleep okay.
And the day after that you're miserably tired all day.
So it reveals, in the stillness and in the quiet, that we're more complicated and unpredictable.
There must be other factors that we're not understanding.
Of course, we have great teachings on karma and cause and effect, so it must all be because of cause and effect, I guess.
But maybe we can't perceive what all the causes are.
We are confused by the effects, with emotions, with energy, with all kinds of stuff.
With the body, that was really true with the body.
We think: I could sit for two periods on a Wednesday night.
Three or four maybe.
Seven to eight will be painful.
Fourteen to twenty-two will be extremely painful.
By twenty-seven I'm in the hospital.
Right?
Linear.
How can it go that way?
I mean, it can be uncomfortable and maybe sometimes there is pain, and I don't mean to belittle anyone who has serious physical conditions.
This can be hard to sit.
But it's not as simple as that.
People sometimes go through phases where there's a ton of pain and they get frustrated and upset, and then just kind of can't take it anymore.
And then eventually something releases or relaxes or changes.
Pain all goes away suddenly.
That's good.
Or it changes or it shifts.
And we start to see the subtle and not so subtle ways that our attitudes and our frame of mind and our emotions and our history are also factors.
It's not just physical mechanics: "Because I have a scoliosis of six degrees, I'm going to be this much pain in these many hours."
It just helps us see that life is so much more rich and complicated and non-understandable than we quite realize.
Which, on a good day, makes us a little more open-minded.
A little more humble.
A little more curious.
What's going to happen next?
Wouldn't it be nice to live with a little curiosity and humility and open-mindedness?
Not throwing away our wisdom or our understanding or our hard-fought knowledge of who we are and what we're about.
It's not wrong exactly, what we think about ourselves.
But if you look carefully, and sesshin sets up situations where you cannot help but look carefully, you can't avoid it, you say, "Well, but all those theories about me are not exactly right either."
Some of both here.
Some of both.
Well, why would you do all this?
Just to learn all this?
Surely there are easier ways to learn all this.
Well, maybe, maybe not.
Another huge, huge benefit of sesshin, I think, which is pretty subtle, is that it shows us that there's deep healing just in the stopping.
Just in the stopping.
Just in Zazen, and Zazen in this context.
Because you would think we would have some yoga.
It would be easier, it would feel good, and it probably would.
But I don't know if I can quite say this clearly.
There's something about just stopping and that's it.
Something this simple, where you're astounded by the end that you usually, not always, feel really good.
You feel like, "Wow, there's been a lot of benefit.
I feel light.
I feel more myself.
I feel grounded.
I feel at ease."
And all I did was sit there.
How could this be?
So it helps to unhook a little bit our striving around improvement.
Maybe that's what I'm trying to say.
It's a sort of radical not improving anything.
You're not doing anything, and yet there's improvement, growth and healing.
So you might still be smart to have a yoga period.
Maybe one day we'll have that.
But there's something, you know what I mean?
There's something about, "Oh, it's the yoga.
The yoga made me feel good.
Okay, now I can stand the Zazen."
It's just straight up.
Where it's difficult, it's easy, it's hard.
It's everything, if we pay attention.
It's not any one thing.
And yet there's benefit, even though we didn't figure it out, we didn't fine-tune it.
It's like a non-optimization.
It's like a kind of freedom from optimization, improvement and clever management and curricula.
You can imagine a much better curricula than this.
It's a non-curricula.
So I guess what I'm saying is that what's great about our way of practice, in the end, is that it's a sort of non-way.
It's a non-method.
A non-technique.
And very strangely, over time, that's deeply healing.
So what do you think?
We've got, oh, not much time left, excuse me.
But what do you think is beneficial?
Why does sesshin help us?
If somebody in this room had never done this before and is now completely terrified, what would you say?
Why is sesshin beneficial?
Or how?
In what way?
**Participant:** I don't know if this directly answers that question, but it certainly does.
Of course, there's change.
Everything changes.
But I think there's also a pattern that, during sesshin, there's a tendency for stillness to build, to accumulate.
And you were saying how maybe the most important part is the breaks.
Maybe also the most important part is the few days later after sesshin, when you still have some contact with that stillness.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
The other thing I love about sesshin a lot is that it's really supportive of direct perception.
And this is available to us all the time.
We don't really see or hear stuff because we're so busy thinking about it, or thinking about something else.
And yeah, that stillness that Talus is talking about.
Sometimes you just see a tree, or a flower, or somebody else sitting there, and you suddenly realize, in a deeply felt way, "That is unbelievable.
That is amazing.
That is so beautiful.
That's beyond what I could ever even describe."
And then you start thinking about it and stop seeing that way.
But you know what I mean?
And this is available all the time.
You walk around, you see beauty everywhere.
You can pay attention.
But it's more available, I think, in sesshin.
But yeah, that's a good point about stillness.
Yeah, Ken.
**Participant:** I was there this weekend at least.
And I got there very early because I was terrified of missing the ferry and getting late.
I got there just after Jeff and one other person showed up, and was there for helping set up.
We were all chatting and talking, and it was loose.
Then we stopped talking, and the projections all paraded in immediately.
People that I got to know reasonably well setting up became different people.
In the silence, they were different people.
Yeah, as soon as the silence came on was one observation.
Another observation, I think, is that sesshin is very slippery.
You think you have something, and then you turn around and... where did that go?
There's a moment of, "Oh..."
Then two minutes later it's like, "What was that?
What was the, oh..."
To me it's like I have it for a minute and I think, "Oh, this is great.
I finally figured something out."
And then it's gone.
There's something there about the way the mind wants to kind of grab onto things, or figure things out.
Yeah.
And I do love the peanut butter cookies, probably.
This is a little weird, but...
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Weird is good.

**Participant:** I've noticed a couple of times after sesshin, when I'm back going to the grocery store, or used to be walking across campus or something like that, I find that people smiled at me more than ever.
I never knew why, but it was true.
I got a different reaction from people, and a more positive reaction from people.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** That makes sense to me.
Yeah, we do it other times.
Yeah, that makes total sense to me.
Do you think you were just noticing it better?
**Participant:** Oh, that's a good question.
Yeah, or both.
No, I don't think so.
I think people were responding to me a little bit differently.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, and if you look around at people at the beginning and the end of sesshin, there's something, you know.
**Participant:** Maybe it's the peacefulness that I had.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** The peacefulness and kind of a glow of some kind, yeah.
I know.
Yeah, Chris.
I believe you.
**Participant:** I go into sesshin, and this isn't to make it sound more scary, but I go into it like it's sort of Zazen 24-7.
So Oryoki is eating Zazen, and breaks are break Zazen, and sleeping is sleeping Zazen.
When I'm having a hard time during my sitting, I find that the non-sitting Zazen helps break through whatever impasse I've got.
So I come back after eating Zazen, and I'm in a different place than I was in Zazen.
Yeah.
And the silence, and the no social interaction, that frame, that container that we create is just sort of so essential to that.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
And the other thing I guess to say about the continuous Zazen is that it also teaches us something about a sort of sustainable effort.
A gentle effort that you can just keep going, and keep going, and keep going.
And that seems like the only way to learn that is experientially.
You can't try too hard for that long.
**Participant:** Yeah, I can be trying so bloody hard on the cushion, but then it's like, ah, I ease up the rest of the time.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Eventually you ease up, yeah.
**Participant:** What terrified me before my first sesshin was that it was silent, because I like talking.
And the thought of not talking for a week was just really strange.
Why do people do that?
And I was totally astounded to realize how much our day-to-day social interactions, how much that is actually draining, how much energy it takes to meet everybody fully every day.
And you never know if someone is going to address you and whether you need to respond.
I could just drop that.
I remember at one point I wanted to turn to someone, "Isn't this sunset so stunning?"
But that person was standing next to me and just staring out.
I didn't need to say it.
You realize that that's just interrupting them.
To realize how much we share in common intention and joint pleasure of being alive.
That was just pretty amazing.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Wonderful, yeah.
It also kind of shows you there are so many different kinds of silence.
Some of us may have been socialized even at a young age to a sort of aversive silence, like a scorning kind of silence.
So this is an interesting way that we can rediscover a kind of companionable silence together, like Chris was talking about.
You don't need to say anything.
Why would you say anything?
It's so clear, we're together and connected in the silence.
Can you say something?
**Participant:** Yeah, I was thinking about what Cal said and about the contacting heart mind.
I just recall the story when I was driving back from Samish three years ago.
You're not checking your phone, and I checked my phone.
My mom said to call, and I called.
And I found out my grandpa passed away on the drive back.
We were just leaving.
I mean, nothing spectacular here to say about it, other than that I felt very open and able to feel what I had to feel about that, and talk to my grandma and hear how she was feeling.
I remember breaking into tears just because I realized that she'll be okay.
That's how I felt talking to her.
But in a certain amount of sensitivity, you think maybe getting news like that after sesshin, you would just go to pieces or something.
But I actually felt quite strong facing that news.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, that's a good example.
Thank you.
I think we always talk about the triple gem, and where can you better find sangha than at sesshin?
We're all together.
And to be in a body like that for a week, it's pretty powerful, I think.
**Participant:** And just all in it together.
I agree with that as well.
It feels like, even though we're silent the entire time, it really feels like we're strengthening our community.
And probably the most powerful thing that I come away with is the interaction where you meet somebody on the path and you both stop and go to the gassho.
And that's just such an amazing thing.
An amazing moment that you share with that person.
I really feel like it's just a lot of love that gets generated in the time together.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, I'm glad you mentioned that, because we're interacting.
It's just interacting in a different sort of way.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.
You're not isolated.
Kate, last one.
**Participant:** In that vein, there was a fellow there that I just did a little work with.
That was also at Indian Ola, anyway, this weekend.
I got on the ferry and I saw his van, and it was like, "Oh, obviously we have this deep relationship or something."
We just interacted for, I don't know, minutes at the sesshin, but somehow there's this tremendous bond developed.
And the other thing is, I'm one of those people Tim talks about that doesn't sleep at night at the sesshin.
It gets to be three o'clock in the morning and I'm going, "Oh my God, this is terrible.
I'm going to be so miserable."
So this sesshin, I thought, I'm really going to see how I really feel throughout the day.
Yeah, I was awake, and then I was just watching through the day.
And it really was not miserable.
It's this pleasant, dreamy sort of state.
And then by the evening, it's pretty trippy, really.
I'll loosen it up a little bit.
But it really was not miserable.
So I have to keep it nice all the time.
And I don't know that I can see that I always leave sesshin in a very joyous state, no matter how miserable I think I am when I'm not sleeping.
It never, ever fails.
In the middle of a sesshin, I think, "I can't do this anymore.
I just can't do this anymore.
I'm just too wiped out."
But always I end in that way.
And I don't know what the cause and effect is.
I don't know what piece of sesshin actually does it, or if it's the whole composite.
But it always ends up there.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Well, that's a nice last note.
Who would have thought just sitting there quietly would be a joyful thing?
Yeah.
